Subject: Reflections on Governance and Labor Relations

Following discussions with the Foreign Office, which operated under the direction of the Chancellor, I wish to share my perspectives on Prince Bismarck’s approach to labor issues. While not antagonistic towards the working classes, Prince Bismarck disagreed with assessments of the Berlin Congress’s outcomes, of which he acted as mediator. He expressed a desire to prevent widespread conflict and felt compelled to offer his services in that capacity.

In subsequent conversations regarding colonial policy, I observed his intention to utilize colonies primarily for commercial exchange, rather than for the benefit of the fatherland or as sources of raw materials. He believed agitation and rebellion should be suppressed, even through the use of force. I, however, aimed to foster positive relations with the German working population and actively pursued this objective. 

I maintained a respectful relationship with my grandmother, acknowledging her extensive experience, but asserted my need for independent action regarding German affairs, particularly during my visit to St. This divergence stemmed from his belief that the social question could be addressed through strict measures and, if necessary, military intervention, a view I did not share. 

From that point forward, my relationship with the Queen improved significantly, and she treated me as an equal sovereign. Count Herbert accompanied me on my initial journeys as a representative of the Foreign Office. I understood that the Prince, despite his accomplishments, ultimately served as my official. He interacted with individuals from all social backgrounds and was held in high regard, and I reciprocated his friendship and gratitude. I convened a Crown Council to address these matters.

Throughout my reign, I demonstrated openness to various political parties, excluding only the most radical socialists, and was not opposed to liberals. Notably, Miquel, a liberal, served as my Finance Minister, Moeller as my Minister of Commerce, and Herr von Benaigsen, a liberal leader, held the position of Chief President of Hanover. 

Regarding our relationship, Tsar Nicholas II believed Prince Bismarck’s departure would improve trust between us. He considered this a positive development, equivalent to saying that, from the time of the Berlin Congress, Bismarck skillfully navigated diplomatic and political challenges for twelve years.

Reports from commanders of summoned troops indicated the situation, and one such report came from a former comrade, von Michaelis of the Hussar Guard Regiment, known for his wit. He engaged with striking workers in a friendly manner, establishing communication and de-escalating tensions. The Prince observed this, remarking on a changing world. This perspective was also evident during Admiral von Tirpitz’s visit to Friedrichsruh, when he sought Bismarck’s support for the first Navy bill. I explained that I could not reconcile such a course with my conscience or my responsibility to address the difficult conditions faced by the laboring classes.

I recall Bismarck entrusting me with the sensitive Brest mission, stating that I “would one day be his own Chancellor,” suggesting his belief in my capabilities. Bismarck possessed a unique ability to manage multiple complex issues simultaneously. I maintained a good and trusting relationship with Prince Bismarck since my assignment to the Foreign Office. An example of the Cabinet’s attitude towards me during that time was the debate over renewing the Socialist Law, a measure devised by Bismarck to combat socialism. Through these interactions, I gained thorough knowledge of agricultural issues and understood the challenges faced by farmers.
